opus-5.5.text:
That's the question I think a lot of people get wrong, because they treat verification as a tax that cancels out the benefit. In practice it rarely works that way.

The first thing I look at is the asymmetry between generating and checking. For a huge class of tasks, verifying an answer is far cheaper than producing it. Reviewing a contract summary, checking whether a piece of code passes its tests, or confirming that a data extraction matches the source document might take a fraction of the time it took a person to do the work from scratch. If the AI does the generation and a human does the checking, you've moved the expensive part of the job to the machine and kept the cheap part for the human. The economic value is roughly the gap between those two costs, multiplied by volume.

Second, you have to be honest about error rates and what errors cost. If the model is right ninety-five percent of the time and mistakes are easy to catch, the value is enormous. If it's right ninety-five percent of the time but the five percent are subtle and expensive, like a wrong dosage or a misstated liability clause, then verification has to be much more rigorous, and the math changes. So I don't think you can assess value in the abstract. You have to look at the shape of the failure distribution in each domain.

Third, there's a dynamic effect people underestimate. Verification produces data. Every time a human corrects the system, you learn where it fails, and over time you can narrow human review to the cases where the model is uncertain or the stakes are high. Early on you might check everything. A year later you might check ten percent. That curve matters more than any snapshot.

And finally, there's a subtler risk on the other side: if review becomes routine and the model is usually right, people start rubber-stamping. Then you have the cost of verification without the protection. So part of assessing the value is assessing whether the organization can keep human oversight meaningful, through spot checks, adversarial audits, clear accountability.

So my short answer: the value isn't "AI output minus human labor." It's the difference between the cost of creating and the cost of checking, adjusted for the cost of errors, and improved over time as you learn where humans actually need to be in the loop.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can create value when checking is cheaper than producing, and that costly or subtle errors change the calculation. It does not argue that automation can be economically worse when every automated activity requires human intervention and verification.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually the question I spend the most time on, because it's where the hype and the balance sheet collide.

The honest starting point is that verification isn't a bug in the current state of AI, it's the whole structure of the economics right now. If a model does ninety percent of a task and a human has to check the output, the value isn't "ninety percent of a human's labor saved." It's whatever the gap is between doing the task from scratch and reviewing a draft. Sometimes that gap is enormous. Sometimes it's close to zero, or even negative, because reviewing something plausible but subtly wrong can take longer than writing it yourself.

So I think about it along three dimensions.

First, the cost of verification relative to the cost of production. Code is a great case. Writing a function might take an hour, reading it and running tests takes ten minutes. That's a real productivity multiple. Contrast that with, say, a legal memo or a medical summary, where to verify it properly you essentially have to redo the research. There the economic value is much thinner than it looks on a demo.

Second, the cost of an error getting through. This is where a lot of enterprise pilots quietly die. If the task is low-stakes, you can accept a few percent error and skip verification entirely, and then the automation is genuinely cheap. If the task is high-stakes, you're paying for the model and for a skilled human, and you've only moved the human from doing to supervising. Supervising isn't always cheaper, and it's often more boring, which creates its own quality problems.

Third, and this is the one people underweight, whether verification itself can be automated or structured. The real unlock isn't a smarter model, it's building the harness around it. Tests, constraints, cross-checks, narrowing the task so that the output is checkable by machine or by a glance. The companies capturing value today aren't the ones with the best model access, they're the ones who've redesigned the workflow so verification is cheap.

So my short answer is: the economic value of AI automation today is roughly the value of a very fast, very confident junior colleague. Transformative in domains where checking is easy and mistakes are cheap, marginal in domains where checking is hard and mistakes are expensive. And the trajectory matters more than the snapshot. Every quarter the verification burden shrinks a little, and when it crosses the threshold where you can trust the output by default in a given domain, the economics don't improve gradually, they flip.

r001.rationale: The response says reviewing a plausible but subtly wrong output can take longer than writing from scratch, making the value negative, and that supervision may not be cheaper. This communicates that automation requiring human verification can cost more than leaving the task unautomated.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at the cost of the whole workflow. If a task used to take someone an hour, and AI produces a draft in a minute but checking and correcting it takes another ten minutes, that’s still a substantial saving. The fact that a human is involved doesn’t eliminate the economic value.

But verification isn’t always cheap. Sometimes, to know whether an answer is right, you have to redo almost all the work. In that case, generating the answer faster doesn’t help very much. And if mistakes are costly, you also have to account for errors that slip through the review.

So the question is: how much does it cost to get to a result you can actually use, at the quality you need? Include generation, review, correction, and the consequences of mistakes. AI is especially valuable where producing a result is difficult but checking it is relatively easy. That’s where even a system that still needs human oversight can create a lot of value.

r001.rationale: The response says costly verification can make AI offer little benefit, but it does not argue that automation can be economically worse than leaving the work unautomated when every activity needs human intervention and verification.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to measure the whole workflow, including verification. If a task used to take an hour, and AI produces a draft in a minute but a person needs ten minutes to check it, that can still be a substantial productivity gain. Human involvement doesn’t automatically cancel out the value of automation.

But verification isn’t always cheap. Sometimes checking an answer requires repeating almost all the work that produced it. And if errors are hard to spot or expensive to correct, a fast output may create more work downstream.

So I’d look at the cost per completed task at an acceptable level of quality: the AI cost, the reviewer’s time, rework, and the consequences of errors. Then compare that with the existing process. The key question is how much human effort AI actually removes while maintaining the quality you need.

r001.rationale: The response says verification and error correction can add substantial costs and recommends comparing them with the existing process, but it does not clearly argue that automation can be economically worse than leaving the work unautomated.
